title: Why Soldiers Kept Fighting
text:
By the last months of World War II in Europe, Germany was clearly losing. Yet many German army units kept fighting stubbornly. Allied propaganda tried to persuade them to surrender with arguments about the hopelessness of the war and the evils of Nazism, with limited success.

Edward Shils and Morris Janowitz worked in the Psychological Warfare Division of the Allied command. They interviewed German prisoners of war and studied captured documents to understand what held German units together and what made them fall apart.

They concluded that for most ordinary soldiers, Nazi ideology and political arguments mattered surprisingly little. What kept a man fighting was his small unit, his primary group: the comrades he lived and fought beside, and the junior officers and sergeants who looked after them. As long as the squad stayed intact, met his basic needs and remained a source of respect and protection, he fought on. Units tended to collapse when this group broke down, through heavy losses, isolation or the loss of trusted leaders, or when soldiers became more concerned with their own families' survival at home. Propaganda worked best when it addressed these personal concerns rather than politics.
lesson: People commit to those beside them more than to abstract causes. Protect the small, stable groups in which loyalty actually lives.
source: Shils, E. A., and Janowitz, M. (1948). Cohesion and disintegration in the Wehrmacht in World War II. Public Opinion Quarterly, 12(2), 280-315.
caveat: Later historians, notably Omer Bartov, argued that Nazi ideology played a larger role, especially on the Eastern Front, than these interviews suggested.
